newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mandela practises what he preaches.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mandela practises what he preaches.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela handed his political rival Mangosuthu Buthelezi the reins of power in his absence from South Africa at the weekend in a tangible demonstration of reconciliation.

While Mandela and his deputy, Thabo Mbeki, were trying to bring Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila together to agree on a transition to democracy, Buthelezi was sworn in as acting president of South Africa for the third time this year.

Buthelezi, although a bitter opponent of Mandela's ruling party, returned the gesture of peace and goodwill, telling reporters he was not a supporter of coups when jokingly asked if he would try to hold onto the position permanently.
"Some people have that idea, but I support democratic processes," he was quoted as saying at his swearing-in ceremony.
But leading political analyst Tom Lodge told Reuters Mandela was misguided if he hoped his efforts at building reconciliation at home would hold water with Mobutu or Kabila.
"If he does have the exemplary reason of showing Kabila and Mobutu the possibility of adversaries working together, it is probably misplaced," Lodge said.

"There would be little to be gained by agreement on a government of national unity in Zaire because anything you put in place will probably fall apart, not very far down the line. It's the most awful country to try to render governable."
Mandela has had a mixed success as a peace broker since he emerged in 1990 from a quarter of a century in jail to lead South Africa from apartheid to democracy.
Alone or in concert with other Southern African leaders, Mandela has contributed to peace-making missions in Angola, Algeria, Lesotho, Swaziland, Burundi, Zaire, Nigeria and Sudan.
But only in Lesotho, a tiny sovereign island within South Africa where he helped to reverse a royal coup and to prevent a military takeover, can he claim unequivocal success.
With Zaire, Mandela has put his personal credibility on the line in brokering the first face-to-face encounter between Mobutu and Kabila on board a South African naval ship.

"This is South Africa's first major foray into African politics and they'd like it work but that is unlikely," said Lodge. "Mobutu has over the past few years shown an amazing capacity for duplicity...and Kabila's probably also a nasty piece of work too.

"All that Mandela and Mbeki can hope to achieve is some kind of halt to the blood-letting and a new administration which doesn't indulge in very vindictive forms of retribution against opponents and, for example, Hutu refugees," Lodge said. "Good luck to them!"

The international community has put pressure on Mandela to use his immense moral authority to turn Africa toward stability, democracy and economic growth. But this has not been unanimously endorsed at home.

The Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a radical black anti- apartheid movement somewhat nullified since the 1994 elections when it garnered just over one percent of the national vote, wants Mandela to focus his energy inside the country.
"We encourage any efforts to bring peace to Africa but his attention should be focused here," PAC Deputy President Motsoko Pheko told Reuters. "Charity begins at home."
